told_more: The record gave me causes, exact dates and the life of every house before 1989, none of which the four frames can show: A's shopfront dates from 1931 and the shop shut in 2009, B burned in 1935 and was rebuilt, all of C's windows were replaced in 1971, D was boarded in 1986 when its owner died, E has stood empty since 1993. It also corrected several stories I had built from the pictures, such as when E was vacated, when A's shop closed and who renewed C's windows. The views only showed the surface of each house at four moments. They are quicker for seeing what changed and where, but they left me guessing at why and when.

misled.claim: A was a working shop through 2010, and the shop closed between 2010 and 2020, which is why the shopfront came out. The record says the shop closed in 2009, so the 2010 frame shows an empty shopfront, and the shopfront was only taken out in 2016 for a flat.

E was a lived-in, kept house in 2000 (care 'kept', confidence 2), and it was vacated between 2000 and 2010. The record says the last owner died and the house was left empty and neglected from 1993; the boards went up in 2008 after a break-in, so it was already empty in 2000.
E's windows were original in 1989 and 2000. The record says the front windows were replaced in 1965.
People may have moved from E to D, so that D's reopening and E's boarding were linked. The record gives separate causes: heirs leaving E empty, and a young family buying D.
D's roof and structure stayed sound while the house stood empty (roof read as original and kept). The record says the roof let in water by 1995.
D had probably stood empty for a long time before 1989. The record says it was boarded in 1986, only three years earlier.
C's windows were old original ones in 1989, and its ground-floor windows were still original until 2020. The record says all of the windows were replaced cheaply in 1971.

C's window renewal was one steady owner doing a bit at a time, the 2020 front windows were the same kind of renewal as the gable window, and C stayed a single family house. The record says the upper flat's owners restored copies of the 1879 windows in 1998, and a different owner, of the ground-floor flat, fitted factory 'old style' windows in the back wall in 2011.
B was extended with a glazed veranda under a balcony, as its business grew. The record holds only a balcony over the lane (2003), and gives no link to the bakery.
2000 to 2010 the corner grew busier. The record gives a mixed picture: a balcony on B, a family at D, but the cafe left A in 2009 because the trade had gone up the hill, and E was boarded.
The frames fall somewhere between 1890 and 1950, a guess made before I was told the years. The record's events run to 2017, so they were 1989 to 2020.

views_showed: At a glance, which houses changed in each decade and how: B's blank shopfront in 2000, then the veranda and balcony in 2010, A's shop window giving way to house windows in 2020, D's boards coming off and E's going on. The same frames show that D and E swap places, one reopening as the other closes, which the record lists as two unrelated entries.

What a change did to the street. B's glazed extension fills the gap beside the lane and shades A's side wall, and A's ground floor returned to the same rhythm of windows as the upper floors, which the record's 'copies of the windows it had covered' does not make visible. A shopfront cut across two bays is plainly a later insertion into a house built with ordinary windows.

C's renewal showing as a visible gradient of window quality, bare, then trimmed at the gable, then trimmed at the front. A viewer can say which windows are renewed, which the record does not say outright for the cheap 1971 ones.

Boarded windows read as emptiness immediately from the lane, even from the city view, and I could pick out D and E from the quay road as the two let-go houses. The record does not show how that looks, or that a house can be boarded for years while its walls and roof look sound from outside.
